items.learnMore:
Affordance versus signifier

An affordance is a real possibility of the element. A signifier is what you can perceive that points to it. Fixing a missed button usually means adding a signifier, not changing behavior.

Common mistake

Saying an element has no affordance because it looks flat. It can still be clickable; it just fails to announce it.

items.learnMore:
Feedback loops

A feedback loop is the visible answer to an action. Without one, people repeat the action to test it, which can cause duplicates and erodes trust.

Common mistake

The pattern's implied promise

Each pattern carries expectations. A toggle promises instant effect. If your setting needs a Save step or takes seconds, pick a pattern that does not promise instantly, or make the change really instant.

Common mistake

Choosing a pattern for its look while ignoring what it implies about timing and reversibility.

Each pattern carries expectations. A toggle promises instant effect. If your setting needs a Save step or takes seconds, pick a pattern that does not promise instantly, or make the change really instant.

Common mistake

Choosing a pattern for its look while ignoring what it implies about timing and reversibility.
items.reflection: Where have you flipped a switch-like control and later found the change had not been applied? What pattern would have set the right expectation?

items.prompt: Which pairing breaks a pattern's promise?
choices: A modal that opens just to show information needing no decision
A checkbox that waits for an explicit Send before anything happens
A toggle that applies the setting at the moment it is flipped
A dropdown that lists several options and lets the user pick one
items.explanation: A modal promises an interruption that needs a decision. Opening one for information that needs none breaks that promise.
items.reference:
What a pattern promises
toggle: change is instant
checkbox: choose now, send later
modal: a decision is needed
broken promise: user trusts the shape, gets surprised
Why: recognising the pattern means trusting its promise, so lying with it costs trust.

items.learnMore:
A visible fallback

The fix adds a permanent circle that is tappable, keeps the swipe as a shortcut, and gives partial feedback during the hold. A coach mark is a good addition but a weak replacement for a permanent cue.

Common mistake

Removing the gesture, or leaving it as the only way in with a one-time hint.
items.reflection: Think of a shortcut you rely on. What visible, slower route sits under it for someone who has never learned it?

items.learnMore:
Novelty and its audience

The original mistake was making the swipe the only way in. Novelty can pay for itself for frequent users, or when paired with an explicit introduction, and the right balance shifts with the audience.

Common mistake

Applying the casual-app answer to a tool used for hours a day, or the reverse.
items.reflection: Consider an audience very different from the one in the case: children, experts, or drivers. What would you keep and what would you drop?
